name: Local Models for Patient Data
title: Local Models for Patient Data
answer: Local models for patient data means AI models that run on hardware inside a hospital, clinic, or other care organization rather than sending patient data to a remote vendor service. They cover tasks such as clinical documentation, coding, image triage, and patient messaging, where the data is sensitive and the organization wants to keep it within its own network. The scope includes the model itself, the runtime, the data pipeline, and the surrounding access controls. It also includes the governance question of whether a locally hosted model is a medical device or a clinical support tool. The site tracks 1000 medical AI models, and local deployment is one pattern among them.

sections.body: Local models for patient data means AI models that run on hardware inside a hospital, clinic, or other care organization rather than sending patient data to a remote vendor service. They cover tasks such as clinical documentation, coding, image triage, and patient messaging, where the data is sensitive and the organization wants to keep it within its own network. The scope includes the model itself, the runtime, the data pipeline, and the surrounding access controls. It also includes the governance question of whether a locally hosted model is a medical device or a clinical support tool. The site tracks 1000 medical AI models, and local deployment is one pattern among them.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: Local models run on servers, workstations, or edge devices owned or leased by the care organization. Common hardware includes GPUs or CPUs with enough memory to hold the model weights and enough storage for logs and updates. The runtime may be a container platform, a model server, or an embedded inference engine. Network isolation, disk encryption, and backup systems are part of the stack. Some deployments use a small model on a clinic workstation, while others use a larger model on a rack server in a data center.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: A team selects a model, tests it on de-identified or synthetic data, and validates it against local patient population characteristics. They then package the model with its dependencies, deploy it to the local environment, and monitor outputs for drift, bias, and errors. Clinical users review outputs before they enter the record, unless the tool is cleared for autonomous use. Updates usually trigger revalidation and change control. The work is a mix of data engineering, clinical informatics, and quality assurance.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Patient data stays on local infrastructure, but that does not remove legal duties under privacy and security rules. Organizations typically document the model's provenance, including training data sources, licenses, and version history. Risks include re-identification, unauthorized access by staff, and silent model failure. If the model influences diagnosis or treatment, it may fall under medical device regulation, and product liability questions can arise. The site tracks 6 active product liability and wrongful death lawsuits against AI companies, and its 215 compliance and regulation pages cover many of these duties.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: Local models are becoming more capable as smaller open weight models improve and hardware becomes more efficient. More care organizations are likely to run a mix of local and cloud models, with local models for sensitive data and cloud models for less sensitive tasks. Regulation and standards for local clinical AI are still developing, and auditability and provenance will matter more. The site tracks 800 scientific models and 732 AI tools, and some of that work will shape what can run locally. The direction is toward tighter integration with the electronic health record and clearer device boundaries.
